title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention
body:
Overview. Scaled dot-product attention is the mixing engine of the transformer: each position asks a question (its query), every position offers a match score against its key, and the scores decide how much of each position's content (its value) gets mixed into the new representation. In one line: softmax(QKT / √d) · V — mix together whoever your questions match.

How it works. Raw match scores are any real numbers, including negatives — not yet a mixing recipe. The softmax pushes them through exp + normalize so the weights are positive and sum to one. The fussy detail: divide the scores by √d (the key dimension) first, or with large dot products softmax collapses into a switch — one position takes everything and the mix dies. Each tile then offers its value vector, and the new tile is the weighted sum of everybody's content, weighted by how much it was listened to. Queries, keys and values stack into matrices Q, K, V, so the whole loop is a single matrix expression.

History. Attention for neural networks was introduced by Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio in 2014 for machine translation; Vaswani et al. made it the whole architecture in “Attention Is All You Need” (2017), adding the √d scaling. It now underlies large language models and vision transformers.

Cross-links. The softmax normalizer is also covered as an activation function in the Activation Functions Database (JAH-ACTFN-000001); this record covers the attention mechanism itself.
demo_code:
import math

def softmax(xs):
    m = max(xs)
    ex = [math.exp(x - m) for x in xs]
    s = sum(ex)
    return [e / s for e in ex]

def attention(Q, K, V, scale=True):
    # Q: n_q x d, K: n_k x d, V: n_k x dv -> n_q x dv
    d = len(Q[0])
    out = []
    weights_all = []
    for q in Q:
        scores = [sum(q[i]*k[i] for i in range(d)) for k in K]
        if scale:
            scores = [s / math.sqrt(d) for s in scores]
        w = softmax(scores)
        weights_all.append(w)
        out.append([sum(w[j]*V[j][c] for j in range(len(K))) for c in range(len(V[0]))])
    return out, weights_all

# 4 image tiles: content vectors (values) and keys; 1 query tile
K = [[1.0, 0.1], [0.2, 1.0], [-1.0, 0.3], [0.0, -1.0]]
V = [[10.0, 0.0], [0.0, 10.0], [-10.0, 0.0], [0.0, -10.0]]
Q = [[0.9, 0.2]]
d = 2

out_s, w_s = attention(Q, K, V, scale=True)
out_u, w_u = attention(Q, K, V, scale=False)

print("scaled dot-product attention: softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)) . V")
print("  d =", d, " raw scores:", ["%.2f" % (sum(Q[0][i]*K[j][i] for i in range(d))) for j in range(4)])
print("  unscaled weights:", ["%.4f" % x for x in w_u[0]], " max =", "%.4f" % max(w_u[0]))
print("  scaled   weights:", ["%.4f" % x for x in w_s[0]], " max =", "%.4f" % max(w_s[0]))
print("  new tile (scaled):", ["%.3f" % x for x in out_s[0]])
assert abs(sum(w_s[0]) - 1.0) < 1e-9 and all(x > 0 for x in w_s[0])
assert abs(sum(w_u[0]) - 1.0) < 1e-9
# the collapse: exaggerate score magnitude and watch softmax become a switch
big = softmax([s*10 for s in [0.92, 0.38, -0.84, -0.20]])
print("  scores x10 -> weights:", ["%.4f" % x for x in big], " (winner-take-all switch)")
assert max(big) > 0.99
print("OK: weights positive, sum to one; scaling decides switch vs mix.")

title: Softmax Function (Attention's Normalizer)
body:
Overview. The softmax turns any list of real scores — positive, negative, or zero — into a mixing recipe: positive weights that sum to exactly one. Push each score through exp, then divide by the total: softmax(x)i = exi / ∑j exj. Negatives are allowed as input; they simply get small weights. It is the normalizer inside attention (see JAH-ATTN-000001) and, as an activation function, is covered in the Activation Functions Database (JAH-ACTFN-000001); this record covers its role as attention's normalizer, not duplicated there.

Behavior. Softmax has a temperature dial: low temperature sharpens the recipe toward a winner-take-all switch, high temperature flattens it toward a uniform blend. In attention the fixed divisor √d plays the temperature's role — skip it and large scores collapse the mix into a switch.

History. The multinomial logistic (softmax) form goes back to Luce (1959); Bridle introduced the name “softmax” for neural networks in 1990.
demo_code:
import math

def softmax(xs, temperature=1.0):
    xs = [x / temperature for x in xs]
    m = max(xs)
    ex = [math.exp(x - m) for x in xs]
    s = sum(ex)
    return [e / s for e in ex]

scores = [2.1, 0.4, -0.7, 1.2]   # raw match scores: any real number
w = softmax(scores)
print("softmax: exp + normalize")
print("  raw scores :", scores)
print("  weights    :", ["%.4f" % x for x in w])
print("  sum        :", "%.6f" % sum(w), " all positive:", all(x > 0 for x in w))
assert abs(sum(w) - 1.0) < 1e-9 and all(x > 0 for x in w)

# negatives are allowed as input; they just get small weights
w2 = softmax([3.0, -2.0])
print("  softmax([3.0, -2.0]) =", ["%.4f" % x for x in w2])
assert abs(sum(w2) - 1.0) < 1e-9

# temperature: low T sharpens toward a switch, high T flattens toward uniform
print("  T=0.2 ->", ["%.3f" % x for x in softmax(scores, 0.2)])
print("  T=5.0 ->", ["%.3f" % x for x in softmax(scores, 5.0)])
print("OK: softmax turns any real scores into a positive mixing recipe summing to one.")
